extracted.intended_audience: poets, fiction writers, and creative nonfiction writers searching for literary magazines to submit to
extracted.subtask_description: A directory-style resource to help writers find literary magazines that publish their work by providing editorial policies, submission guidelines, reading periods, genres, and editorial preferences for hundreds of journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial policies / submission guidelines / contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Each magazine listing includes editorial policies, submission guidelines, and contact information—everything you need to know before submitting your work to determine which publications match your vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided policies and guidelines on a magazine's listing to check eligibility, formatting, simultaneous submissions, fees (if any), and how to contact editors before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use site filters for reading period and submission status
rubrics_metrics.description: Filters allow finding magazines with reading periods that are open now or opening soon (within the next thirty days) and magazines that accept unsolicited submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply filters to surface only magazines currently accepting work or matching your desired timeline; useful to avoid submitting when a journal is closed or by invitation only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading period (dates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each magazine lists its reading period(s) with start and end dates (e.g., Jan 1 to Dec 31; Feb 1 to Mar 31).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit only within a journal’s stated reading period; some journals have multiple windows per year and some accept year-round submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazines explicitly list the genres they publish—common examples on the page include Poetry, Fiction, Creative Nonfiction, Translation, and Review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm that your piece’s genre matches the magazine’s stated genres before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subgenre and topical preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Many listings include subgenres or topical focuses (e.g., flash fiction, lyric essay, BIPOC Voices, experimental, speculative, micro-poetry, narrative nonfiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match your work to the magazine’s subgenre tags or thematic calls (e.g., a magazine tagged 'flash fiction' favors very short stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Length/format limits (explicit word/line counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals specify precise length/format requirements—for example: 32 Poems prefers work that fits on a single page (32 lines or less); 100 Word Story enforces a 100-word format; After Dinner Conversation publishes short stories 1,500 to 7,000 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow a magazine’s length and format limits exactly (line counts, word counts, or strict forms) to avoid automatic rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic or guest-edited issue focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain journals organize issues around themes or use guest editors (e.g., About Place Journal’s themed issues guest-edited by fellows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check current or upcoming themes and guest-editor calls; submit pieces that engage a theme when appropriate or wait for a fitting issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for particular voices or communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Some magazines explicitly prioritize work from specific communities—examples: Acentos Review publishes Latinx writers (accepts English, Spanish, Spanglish); AC|DC aims to feature queer voices; #TWP Quarterly is curated by teens to amplify youth voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to identity- or community-focused journals and consider whether your perspective aligns with their mission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic or institutional focus
rubrics_metrics.description: A few journals limit or prefer contributors based on geography or institutional affiliation (e.g., Acorn Review publishes work by residents of San Diego County; 30 North welcomes North Central College students and alumni).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm any geographic or institutional eligibility before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Some titles specify which languages or multilingual submissions they accept (e.g., Acentos Review welcomes English, Spanish, Spanglish; Acorn: a Journal of Contemporary Haiku showcases English-language haiku).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit in the accepted language(s) or translations when allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial taste and stylistic preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual journals describe aesthetic preferences—examples include 2River View (prefers poems with image, subtlety, and point of view; a surface of worldly exactitude and depth of semantic ambiguity), 32 Poems (inventive language with music, form, and feeling), Adroit Journal (bizarre, authentic, subtle, outrageous, indefinable, raw, paradoxical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read back issues to confirm a journal’s taste and tailor submissions to align with their described qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance model and open/closed status
rubrics_metrics.description: Listings indicate whether a journal is open to submissions, temporarily closed, or has rolling/annual windows (e.g., 'Temporarily Closed to Submissions').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect a journal’s open/closed status; do not submit when they are closed and watch for re-open announcements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for experimental / cross-genre work
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple journals explicitly welcome experimental, cross-genre, or formally adventurous work (tags like 'experimental', 'cross-genre', 'post-human', 'surreal', 'weird').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your work is formally experimental, target journals that explicitly state they value such approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on accessibility or readership orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals describe the audience or accessibility they aim for—e.g., Abandoned Mine is aimed at readers 'who don’t yet know they like poetry' (suggesting accessible work); Poetry Is Currency prioritizes poems that mean the most to the author regardless of marketability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a journal’s stated readership or mission when deciding if your voice and approach are a fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication format and frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Listings sometimes note whether a title is online or print and its frequency (e.g., annual print journal, quarterly online).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of format and frequency differences—online vs. print, annual vs. quarterly—when considering exposure and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic or career-stage targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Some publications target particular career stages or demographics (e.g., magazines that identify as amplifying emerging writers, student-run journals, teen-focused magazines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target publications whose contributor base aligns with your career stage or intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission- or value-driven editorial stance
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain journals foreground political or philosophical stances (e.g., Poetry Is Currency’s anticapitalist stance; journals dedicated to earth/spirit/society causes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your work engages a journal’s political/philosophical commitments, highlight that alignment in the submission if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific content signals in blurbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Magazine blurbs often include concrete signals about desired content (e.g., After Happy Hour prefers fiction that leans toward the weird and poetry with strong emotion or a sense of narrative rather than poems that 'play with language' alone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these short editorial blurbs as quick heuristics to determine fit before reading full guidelines or back issues.
